drills.q: Define SRP using the actor-based definition, not 'one method per class'.
drills.a: A class should have one reason to change, meaning one actor/stakeholder whose requirements drive changes to it — a class can have many methods and still satisfy SRP if they all serve one actor.

drills.q: You see a class OrderProcessor with validation, pricing, persistence, and email notification all inline. Name the actors and the SRP violation.
drills.a: Four actors: product/business rules, finance, DBA, marketing. Each drives changes to the same file for unrelated reasons, causing PR collisions and untestable pricing logic without a live DB/email client.

drills.q: What is the honest counter-argument to SRP, and name the anti-pattern it produces when overapplied.
drills.a: Overapplying SRP to domain entities produces the anemic domain model — logic stripped from entities into external services, breaking encapsulation of invariants.

drills.q: When would you deliberately NOT introduce a strategy pattern despite an if/elif chain technically violating OCP?
drills.a: When there are only 2-3 known variants with no evidence of more coming — the abstraction costs more reading time than the conditional, and introducing it is speculative generality (YAGNI violation).

drills.q: A ReadOnlyCache implements a mutable Cache interface by raising NotImplementedError on set(). What's wrong and how do you fix it?
drills.a: LSP violation — callers relying polymorphically on Cache.set() get a runtime surprise. Fix: split into Readable/Writable protocols so ReadOnlyCache only implements Readable, making the illegal call a type error instead of a runtime exception.

drills.q: Name the real anti-pattern caused by overapplying ISP, and describe its symptom.
drills.a: Interface bloat — one interface per method (IReadable, IWritable, IDeletable, IListable), forcing callers to compose many narrow types and making generic code hard to write; documented as a named anti-pattern from enterprise Java.

drills.q: Distinguish Dependency Inversion Principle from dependency injection as a mechanism.
drills.a: DIP: high-level and low-level modules should both depend on an abstraction the high-level module owns conceptually. DI: a runtime mechanism (constructor/setter/framework) for supplying a concrete implementation of that abstraction. You can follow DIP with manual constructor injection and no framework at all.

drills.q: Your team lead insists on 'always follow SOLID, it's best practice.' Give a staff-level pushback that isn't dismissive.
drills.a: Agree on the goal (cheap, safe change), then ask which axis of change is actually live in this code and apply only the principle(s) addressing it — citing e.g. an interface-per-implementation pattern in the repo's own git history that has never had a second implementation land, as evidence the ceremony isn't earning its cost.

drills.q: Design the tool-interface boundary for an agent's tool registry. Which SOLID principle is load-bearing and which is most likely to be misapplied?
drills.a: OCP is load-bearing — new tools register rather than edit a dispatcher. ISP is most likely misapplied if every tool is forced to implement cancel()/estimate_cost()/supports_streaming() even when irrelevant; query capability via isinstance/protocol checks instead of a monolithic Tool interface.

drills.q: What two conditions justify skipping DIP (injecting an abstraction) entirely for a dependency?
drills.a: Exactly one implementation with no plan for a second, and no test-isolation need a manual fake couldn't satisfy without the extra interface/container indirection.
